why_how.text: Bicyclists are easy to crowd, so the law sets a minimum passing space on every road.
Special signs tell you about road types, crossings and slow vehicles before you reach them.

scenario.text: On a narrow two-lane road, Theo comes up behind a bicyclist riding near the middle of the lane, and a Bicycle May Use Full Lane sign is posted.

reasoning.text: The bicyclist may ride mid-lane where the right side is unsafe, and Theo must leave at least three feet of clearance to pass.

result.text: Theo waits until he can give at least three feet of room, then passes safely.

claim.text: Common mistake: thinking the three-foot passing rule applies only where a Pass sign is posted.

correction.text: Drivers must leave at least three feet when passing a bicyclist on any road, whether or not a sign is posted.

memory_support.text: Three feet, every road, every time.

prompt.text: You are passing a bicyclist on a road with no signs at all. What clearance must you leave?

rationale.text: The three-foot minimum applies on any road, whether or not a Pass sign is posted.

narration.text: This chapter moves from signals and signs into special signs, pavement markings and lane controls. We start with a set of special signs that help you share the road. You will learn how route marker shapes tell you what kind of road you are on, what bicycle and pedestrian crossing signs mean, the three-foot rule for passing bicyclists, what a Bicycle May Use Full Lane sign reminds you, and how to recognize a slow-moving vehicle. Several of these rules are about bicyclists, who have the same right to the road as drivers and are much more exposed in a collision.

lines.text: Route sign shape shows the road type.
Yellow signs mark bike and walker crossings.

narration.text: The shape of a route sign or marker tells you what kind of road you are on: an Interstate, a U.S. highway, a State highway or a County highway. Learning the shapes helps you navigate and understand what kind of traffic to expect. Bicycle and pedestrian crossing signs are black symbols on yellow. They mark places, such as where a shared use path meets a road, where both bicyclists and walkers may cross. When you see one, slow down and look for people approaching the road from the side, because they may be crossing at a spot with no traffic signal.

lines.text: At least three feet of clearance.
With or without a posted sign.

narration.text: When passing or overtaking a bicyclist on any road, a driver must leave at least three feet of clearance. That rule applies whether or not a white Pass sign showing the three-foot minimum is posted. The sign is only a reminder. Three feet is a minimum, not a target, so give more room when you can, especially at higher speeds or when the bicyclist may need to swerve around debris. If you cannot give at least three feet, slow down and wait behind the bicyclist until it is safe to pass. A few seconds of patience protects a rider who has no protection of their own.

lines.text: Bicyclists may use the full lane.
When the right side is unsafe.

narration.text: Here is the trap. Many drivers believe a bicyclist must always stay at the far right edge. A white Bicycle May Use Full Lane sign reminds drivers that a bicyclist may ride in the middle of the lane when hazards or poor visibility would make riding on the right side unsafe. That is legal, not rude. Treat a mid-lane bicyclist like any slower vehicle and pass only with at least three feet of room. Another slow road user is marked by a reflective orange triangle on the back, which means the vehicle is built to travel slower than twenty-five miles per hour.

Here is a quick check: you are driving on a quiet county road with no signs at all, and you come up behind a bicyclist. You want to pass. How much clearance must you leave, and does the lack of a sign change anything? Think about it before reading on. You must leave at least three feet of clearance. That rule applies on any road, whether or not a Pass sign is posted. If the bicyclist moves toward the middle of the lane because the edge is rough or unsafe, that is allowed, and you still need at least three feet to pass.

lines.text: Three feet to pass a bicyclist.

narration.text: Let us review. The shape of a route sign or marker tells you whether you are on an Interstate, U.S., State or County highway. Black-on-yellow bicycle and pedestrian crossing signs mark places where both bicyclists and walkers may cross. When passing a bicyclist on any road, leave at least three feet of clearance, whether or not a sign is posted. A Bicycle May Use Full Lane sign reminds you that bicyclists may ride mid-lane when the right side is unsafe. A reflective orange triangle marks a vehicle built to travel slower than twenty-five miles per hour. Next, disabled parking.

why_how.text: Disabled spaces and van-access areas exist so people with disabilities can get in and out of vehicles safely.
Misuse is punished heavily because taking a space can stop a person with a disability from reaching services.

scenario.text: Jess borrows her grandfather's car, which has his disabled placard, to pick up groceries alone.

reasoning.text: A disabled space may be used only when the placard holder is getting in or out, and using someone else's placard brings heavy penalties.

result.text: Jess parks in a regular space, because her grandfather is not with her.

claim.text: Common mistake: thinking a vehicle with a placard may park in the crosshatched area when the disabled spaces are full.

correction.text: A van-access crosshatch beside a disabled space is never a parking spot, even for a vehicle with a placard.

prompt.text: Every disabled space is full and you have a valid placard. May you park in the crosshatched area beside one?

answer.text: No. The crosshatched area is for van access only.

rationale.text: No one may park on the van-access crosshatch at any time, even with a placard.

narration.text: Disabled parking spaces are among the most clearly marked spots in any parking lot, yet they are misused often. This lesson explains who may park in them, what the crosshatched area beside them is for, when a vehicle with a placard may actually use a space, and the penalties for parking without a placard or with someone else's. These rules show up in practice questions, often as short scenarios about borrowed cars, full lots or quick errands. In each case, the answer depends on who is in the car and whether they need the space at that moment.

lines.text: Signs and painted markings reserve the space.
For vehicles showing a disabled permit.

narration.text: Disabled parking signs, and markings painted in the space, reserve those spots for vehicles showing a disabled parking permit, such as a placard or a special license plate. The reservation applies at all times the sign is posted, not only during busy hours. A quick stop of a minute or two is not an exception, and neither is an empty lot. These spaces are usually placed closest to entrances and are often wider, because the people who need them may use wheelchairs, walkers or other mobility aids. Taking one, even briefly, can block someone who truly depends on it.

The crosshatched area next to a disabled space is for van access only, and no one may park there at any time. It gives room for a wheelchair lift or ramp to unfold from the side of a van, and for a person to move between the vehicle and the walkway. If a car parks on the crosshatch, a wheelchair user may be unable to get back into their own van. The rule has no exceptions for short stops, motorcycles or late nights. Treat the crosshatch as part of the space's equipment, not as extra parking. Leave the crosshatch clear for the people who need it.

lines.text: Park only when the holder gets in or out.

narration.text: Here is the trap, in two parts. First, a placard in the car is not enough. You may park in a disabled space only when the person who holds the placard is getting into or out of the vehicle. A family member running errands alone in the holder's car may not use the space. Second, a van-access crosshatch beside a disabled space is never a parking spot, even for a vehicle with a placard. When every disabled space is taken, the crosshatch still stays clear. Questions often test one of these points by describing a placard holder who is not present, or a full lot.

lines.text: Fine, jail, license loss or impoundment.

narration.text: Parking in a disabled space without a placard or plate can be charged as a misdemeanor, with a fine of three hundred fifty to five thousand dollars on conviction, plus possible jail, loss of driving privileges or impoundment of the car. Using somebody else's placard or plate is punished even more heavily: jail time, loss of driving privileges, towing and fines twice the normal amounts. The penalties reflect how much harm misuse can cause. A person with a disability who cannot find a usable space may be unable to reach a doctor, a pharmacy or a job, and borrowing a placard is treated as a deliberate abuse.

Here is a quick check: you hold a valid disabled placard, and when you arrive at the pharmacy, every disabled space is taken. The crosshatched area beside one of the spaces is empty. May you park there? Think it through before reading on. No. The crosshatched area next to a disabled space is for van access only, and no one may park there at any time, even with a placard. You will need to find another space. And remember the other side of the rule: a disabled space may be used only when the placard holder is getting into or out of the vehicle.

Let us review. Disabled parking signs and markings reserve spaces for vehicles showing a disabled parking permit. The crosshatched area next to a disabled space is for van access only, and no one may park there, even with a placard. You may park in a disabled space only when the placard holder is getting into or out of the vehicle. Parking there without a placard or plate can be a misdemeanor with fines, possible jail, loss of privileges or impoundment, and using someone else's placard brings jail, license loss, towing and double fines. Next, we begin pavement markings with yellow lines.

why_how.text: Yellow lines separate opposite directions, so they control the most dangerous move on a two-lane road: passing into oncoming traffic.
The solid yellow exceptions let you turn into driveways and give bicyclists room without creating head-on risk.

scenario.text: Ava is behind a slow tractor on a two-lane road; the yellow lines show a broken line on her side and a solid line on the other side.

reasoning.text: In a mixed pair, only the line on your side counts, so a broken line on her side allows passing when safe.

result.text: Ava passes when the oncoming lane is clear and returns to her lane before the broken line becomes solid.

claim.text: Common mistake: thinking any solid yellow line in a mixed pair forbids passing for everyone.

correction.text: Only the line nearest you counts: solid on your side means no passing, broken on your side means passing is allowed when safe.

prompt.text: A solid and a broken yellow line run side by side, and the solid line is on your side. May you pass?

rationale.text: In a mixed pair only the line nearest you counts, and solid on your side means no passing.

narration.text: Pavement markings are a language painted on the road, and yellow lines are among the most important words. They tell you when passing is allowed on a road with traffic coming toward you, which is one of the riskiest moves in driving. This lesson starts with what pavement markings do in general, then covers broken yellow lines, solid yellow lines, the mixed pair of one solid and one broken line, and the two exceptions that let you cross a solid yellow line. By the end, you should be able to read any yellow line combination and know whether you may pass.

lines.text: Show where passing and lane changes are allowed.
Mark turn lanes, walkways and stop points.

narration.text: Pavement lines and symbols divide lanes, show where passing and lane changes are allowed, mark turn lanes and pedestrian walkways, and show where to stop for signals or signs. They work together with signs, and sometimes they are the only guidance you get, such as on a long rural road with few signs. Color matters. Yellow lines divide traffic going in opposite directions. A broken yellow line means passing is allowed, when it is safe. So the first thing a yellow line tells you is that the traffic on the other side of it is coming toward you.

A solid yellow line, or a pair of solid yellow lines, means no passing. There is one exception in the same rule: you may pass a bicyclist with at least three feet of room when the oncoming lane is clear. That exception exists because a bicyclist moves slowly, and making a car wait behind one for miles can lead to riskier passes later. Still, it only applies when the oncoming lane is truly clear and you can give the full three feet. Passing a slow car or truck across a solid yellow line is not allowed, no matter how clear the road looks.

lines.text: Solid on your side: no passing.
Broken on your side: pass when safe.

narration.text: Sometimes a solid and a broken yellow line run side by side. In that case, you may not pass if the solid line is on your side, but you may pass safely if the broken line is on your side. When you do pass, return to your lane before the broken line becomes solid. This setup is common on hills and curves, where drivers in one direction can see far enough ahead to pass and drivers in the other direction cannot. The line closest to you is the one painted for your direction of travel, so it is the one that tells you what you may do.

lines.text: Look at the line nearest you.

narration.text: Here is the trap. When learners see a solid yellow line anywhere in a pair, they often assume passing is banned for everyone. But in a mixed yellow pair, only the line nearest you counts. Solid on your side means no passing. Broken on your side means passing is allowed when safe. Practice questions describe the pair and ask whether you may pass, and the trick is noticing which side the solid line is on. Picture yourself in the driver seat and look at the line closest to your car. That one line decides your answer. Picture your own seat.

lines.text: Left turn into a driveway, alley or private road.
Around a bicyclist with three feet.

narration.text: Crossing a solid yellow line is allowed, when safe, in two situations. The first is a left turn into a driveway, an alley or a private road. You are not passing anyone; you are leaving the road. The second is getting around a bicyclist with three or more feet of room. Those are the two exceptions, and both require that it be safe. Neither allows you to pass a slow car or truck. When a question offers a reason to cross a solid yellow line, check whether it is one of these two. If it is not, the answer is that crossing is not allowed.

lines.text: The solid line is nearest you.

narration.text: Here is a quick check: on a two-lane highway, you see a solid yellow line and a broken yellow line side by side. The solid line is on your side. The road ahead looks clear. May you pass the slow car in front of you? Decide before reading on. No. In a mixed yellow pair, only the line nearest you counts, and solid on your side means no passing. If the broken line were on your side, you could pass when safe and return before the line turned solid. And a solid yellow line may be crossed only to turn left into a driveway, alley or private road, or to get around a bicyclist with room.

lines.text: Broken: pass when safe. Solid: no passing.

narration.text: Let us review. Pavement lines and symbols divide lanes, show where passing and lane changes are allowed, mark turn lanes and walkways, and show where to stop. Yellow lines divide traffic going in opposite directions. A broken yellow line means passing is allowed. A solid yellow line or pair means no passing, except around a bicyclist with at least three feet of room when the oncoming lane is clear. In a mixed pair, only the line on your side counts. You may also cross solid yellow, when safe, to turn left into a driveway, alley or private road. Next come white lines.

why_how.text: White lines separate lanes going the same way, so they tell you when a lane change is allowed.
Crosswalk rules protect pedestrians, who cannot be seen easily behind stopped vehicles.

scenario.text: On a four-lane road, the car in the lane beside Max stops suddenly at a crosswalk.

reasoning.text: You may not pass a vehicle stopped at a crosswalk; on a multi-lane road you stop behind the crosswalk in your lane.

result.text: Max stops behind the crosswalk and sees a child crossing in front of the stopped car.

claim.text: Common mistake: thinking yellow and white lines both separate traffic going opposite ways.

correction.text: Yellow separates opposite directions, while white separates lanes going your way.

prompt.text: The car in the next lane has stopped at a crosswalk, and you cannot see why. What should you do?

answer.text: Stop behind the crosswalk; do not pass the stopped car.

rationale.text: A pedestrian may be crossing out of sight, and pedestrians have the right of way in crosswalks.

narration.text: In this lesson we move from yellow to white lines, then to markings for bicyclists and the rules at crosswalks. White lines tell you about lanes going the same direction as you, and whether you may change lanes. Green paint, sharrows and conflict zones help drivers and bicyclists share the road. Crosswalks, marked or unmarked, are where pedestrians have the right of way, and one crosswalk rule protects people who are hidden by other vehicles. As we go, notice how each marking tells you who else is using the road near you and what they may do.

lines.text: Separate lanes going the same way.
Broken white: lane change when safe.
Solid white: stay in lane; marks shoulder.

narration.text: White lines separate lanes moving the same way. A broken white line allows a safe lane change. A solid white line means stay in your lane, and a solid white line also marks the road shoulder. So if you see a solid white line between you and the next lane, you should not change lanes there, which is common near intersections and on freeway ramps. Before any lane change across a broken white line, still signal and check your mirrors and blind spot. The line allows the move; it does not guarantee that the space is clear.

Here is the trap. Line color answers who is beside you. Yellow separates opposite directions. White separates lanes going your way. Learners sometimes mix them up, especially at night or on a wide road with several lanes. A practice question may describe a white line and ask whether oncoming traffic is on the other side. The answer is no; white means the traffic beside you is moving the same direction. If the line were yellow, you would know that crossing it could put you in front of oncoming traffic. Always check the color before deciding what a line allows.

lines.text: Green paint: bicycle lanes and areas.
Sharrows: lane may be too narrow to share.

narration.text: Green paint marks a lane or area set aside for bicyclists and makes riders more visible. Sharrows, or shared lane markings, warn that a lane may be too narrow for a car and a bicycle side by side, and bicyclists may ride in the center of such a lane, or whenever they must avoid obstacles or be seen. Conflict zones are broken lines in a bike or bus lane warning drivers and bicyclists that their paths will cross there, for example where cars turn across a bike lane. In a conflict zone, look carefully for bicyclists before you cross their lane, and yield to them.

lines.text: Pedestrians have the right of way.
Slow down or stop as needed.

narration.text: A crosswalk, marked or unmarked, is where pedestrians have the right of way, and drivers must slow down or stop as needed for people crossing in it. An unmarked crosswalk exists at many intersections even when no lines are painted, typically where sidewalks meet the road. So the absence of paint does not remove a pedestrian's right of way. When approaching any intersection, look for people waiting at the curb or stepping off it. Slowing early gives you time to stop smoothly, and it signals to pedestrians that you have seen them and will let them cross.

lines.text: Vehicle stopped at a crosswalk ahead?
Stop behind the crosswalk in your lane.

narration.text: If a vehicle ahead is stopped at a crosswalk, you may not pass it. Stop behind it, or, on a multi-lane road, stop behind the crosswalk in the next lane. The reason is simple: the stopped vehicle may be blocking your view of a pedestrian who is crossing in front of it. If you pass, you could drive straight into that person just as they step into your lane. This rule applies even when you cannot see anyone. Assume the other driver stopped for a reason, and wait until the crosswalk is clear before you move forward. Wait until the crosswalk is clear.

lines.text: Next lane stops at a crosswalk.

narration.text: Here is a quick check: you are driving in the right lane of a four-lane road. The car in the left lane beside you suddenly stops at a crosswalk, and you cannot see anyone crossing. What should you do? Decide before reading on. Stop behind the crosswalk in your lane. You may not pass a vehicle stopped at a crosswalk, because a pedestrian may be crossing out of your sight in front of it. Pedestrians have the right of way in crosswalks, marked or unmarked, and drivers must slow down or stop as needed for people crossing.

lines.text: Bike markings: green, sharrows, conflict zones.

narration.text: Let us review. White lines separate lanes going the same way: a broken white line allows a safe lane change, and a solid white line means stay in your lane and marks the shoulder. Yellow separates opposite directions, white separates lanes going your way. Green paint marks bike areas, sharrows warn a lane may be too narrow to share side by side, and conflict zones mark where drivers and bicyclists cross. Pedestrians have the right of way in crosswalks, marked or unmarked, and you may not pass a vehicle stopped at a crosswalk. Next come restricted lanes.

why_how.text: Keeping right and within one lane makes your position predictable to every other road user.
Restricted lanes keep buses, bicycles and carpools moving, so drivers must check signs before entering them.

scenario.text: A delivery driver wants to stop for a minute in a bike lane to drop off a package.

reasoning.text: Drivers may not drive, idle, park in or otherwise block a bike lane, which is only for bicyclists and authorized users.

result.text: The driver finds a legal parking spot instead and walks the package over.

claim.text: Common mistake: assuming any lane with a white diamond is an HOV lane you can use with a passenger.

correction.text: A white diamond can mark an HOV lane or another restricted lane, so read the sign to learn who may use it.

prompt.text: You see a white diamond painted in a lane ahead. How do you find out whether you may use it?

answer.text: Read the sign to learn who may use the lane.

rationale.text: A white diamond can mark an HOV lane or another restricted lane, and the sign states who may use it.

narration.text: This lesson covers where you should be on the road and which lanes are off limits. You will start with the general rule for lane position and how it applies on roads with no markings at all. Then you will learn about restricted lanes, which are reserved for special uses: bike lanes, transit lanes for buses or light rail, and High Occupancy Vehicle lanes for carpools. Many of these lanes are marked with a white diamond, which means different things in different places. Knowing the rules keeps you out of lanes meant for others, and protects the people using them.

lines.text: Drive on the right half of the road.
Unmarked road: just right of center.

narration.text: As a general rule, drive on the right half of the road and keep to a single lane without straddling two. Straddling lanes confuses other drivers about where you are going and blocks two lanes at once. On a road with no lane signs or markings, drive just right of the center, stay off the shoulder, and follow the same passing and turning rules as on marked roads. Unmarked roads are common in rural areas and new developments. The missing paint does not remove the rules; it just means you have to apply them from memory rather than from the lines in front of you.

Restricted lanes, such as transit or bicycle lanes, are reserved for a special use shown by signs or markings. Often the marking is a white diamond painted in the lane, or a sign at the roadside. Transit lanes are parts of the street marked for buses or light rail, sometimes with limited use by other vehicles allowed, such as turning at the next corner. High Occupancy Vehicle lanes carry a painted white diamond, and signs state which vehicles may use them and how many occupants each needs. When you see a restricted lane, read the signs before you enter, and stay out if they do not include you.

lines.text: Only for bicyclists and authorized users.
Never drive, idle, park or block.

narration.text: Bike lanes are only for bicyclists and other authorized users, who have the right of way there. Drivers may not drive, idle, park in or otherwise block a bike lane. That includes a quick stop to drop off a passenger or a package. When a car blocks a bike lane, the bicyclist is forced into traffic, which is exactly the danger the lane was built to prevent. A bike lane also continues through an intersection even where no paint joins the two sides. So when turning across an intersection, treat the bike lane as if it were painted all the way through.

lines.text: HOV lane or another restricted lane.

narration.text: Here is the trap. A white diamond can mark an HOV lane or another restricted lane, such as a transit lane. Drivers who see a diamond often assume it is a carpool lane and enter as long as they have a passenger. But the diamond alone does not tell you who may use the lane. The sign does. It may limit the lane to buses, to vehicles with a certain number of occupants, or to certain hours. When a practice question mentions a white diamond, the safe answer is to read the sign and follow what it says, rather than to guess from the diamond itself.

lines.text: Limited use by others sometimes allowed.
HOV: signs set vehicles and occupants.

narration.text: Transit lanes are marked by signs and markings for buses or light rail. Sometimes limited use by other vehicles is allowed, for example to turn right at the next intersection, but only as the signs describe. High Occupancy Vehicle lanes are marked with a painted white diamond, and signs state which vehicles may use them and how many occupants each needs. Some HOV lanes need two people, others three, and some allow certain vehicles at any time. Because the rules differ from place to place, reading the sign each time is the only reliable way to know whether you may use the lane.

lines.text: A white diamond in the lane.

narration.text: Here is a quick check: on a busy city street, you notice a white diamond painted in the right lane ahead. You have one passenger. May you use the lane? Think it through before reading on. You cannot tell from the diamond alone. A white diamond can mark an HOV lane or another restricted lane, such as a transit lane, so read the sign to learn who may use it. If the sign limits the lane to buses, or requires more occupants than you have, stay out. And never drive, idle or park in a bike lane, whatever the markings beside it.

lines.text: Read the sign at a diamond.

narration.text: Let us review. Drive on the right half of the road and keep to a single lane. On unmarked roads, drive just right of center, stay off the shoulder, and use the usual passing and turning rules. Restricted lanes are shown by signs or markings, often a white diamond. Bike lanes are for bicyclists, who have the right of way there, and drivers may not drive, idle, park in or block them; they continue through intersections even without paint. Transit lanes serve buses or light rail, and HOV signs state which vehicles and how many occupants may use the lane. Next, center turn and reversible lanes.

why_how.text: A center turn lane gives left-turning drivers a safe place to wait without blocking through traffic.
Reversible lanes add capacity in the busy direction, so their markings must be read carefully.

scenario.text: Kai is driving on a street with a two-way left-turn lane and wants to turn left into a store two blocks ahead.

reasoning.text: Every left turn on that street must be made from the center lane, which is only for waiting to turn, not for traveling.

result.text: Kai stays in the through lane until just before the store, then moves into the center lane, waits for a gap, and turns.

claim.text: Common mistake: using an empty center turn lane to pass slow traffic or drive along for a block.

correction.text: A center turn lane is for waiting to turn left, not for passing or driving along.

prompt.text: Traffic is crawling and the center turn lane is empty. May you drive in it for a block to get ahead?

rationale.text: The center turn lane is only for waiting to turn left, never for passing or traveling.

narration.text: Some roads use their middle lanes in special ways. This lesson covers the two-way left-turn lane, often called the center turn lane, the reversible lane, which changes direction at different times of day, and the diverging diamond interchange, which briefly shifts traffic to the opposite side of the road. Each design solves a traffic problem, but each also has rules that are easy to break if you do not know them. We will pay special attention to telling a reversible lane apart from a center turn lane, because their markings can look similar at a glance.

lines.text: Only for left turns from either direction.
Wait in it until the turn is safe.

narration.text: A two-way left-turn lane, or center turn lane, is only for drivers turning left from either direction. You may wait in it until the turn is safe, but you may not use it to pass or to travel. If a street has a shared center turn lane, every left turn must be made from that lane and not from any other. That rule clears the through lanes of stopped turning cars, which reduces rear-end crashes. Enter the center lane shortly before your turn, signal, and wait for a gap in oncoming traffic. Remember that drivers from the other direction may also be using the same lane.

lines.text: Center lane: waiting to turn left.

narration.text: Here is the first trap. When traffic is slow and the center turn lane is empty, it is tempting to use it to get ahead. A center turn lane is for waiting to turn left, not for passing or driving along. It also removes the option of turning left from other lanes, so you cannot turn left from a through lane on that street. Using the center lane as a travel lane is dangerous, because drivers from the other direction may enter it to turn left toward you. Move into it only when you are about to turn, and leave it by turning.

lines.text: One way at some times, the other at others.
Barrier or double broken yellow lines.

narration.text: Reversible lanes carry traffic one way at some times and the other way at other times, often to add capacity toward downtown in the morning and away from it in the evening. They are set apart by a barrier or by double broken yellow lines, sometimes with signs or special lights over the lane showing which direction may use it at the moment. Before entering a reversible lane, check the signs or lights every time, because the lane you used this morning may be carrying oncoming traffic this afternoon. Never assume the direction from memory.

lines.text: Center turn lane: left turns only.

narration.text: Here is the second trap. Double broken yellow lines signal a reversible lane, which differs from a center turn lane used only for left turns. A driver who mistakes a reversible lane for a center turn lane might wait in it to turn, just as a stream of traffic is assigned to that lane. A driver who mistakes a center turn lane for a reversible lane might drive along in it. Check the lines and the signs. Double broken yellow lines and overhead lights point to a reversible lane, while center turn lanes carry their own markings and are only for turning left.

lines.text: Traffic shifts to the opposite side.

narration.text: A diverging diamond interchange shifts traffic to the opposite side of the road across the interchange so vehicles can move onto freeway ramps without interruption. For a short stretch, you drive on the left side of the road, with oncoming traffic on your right, before the road crosses back. This design removes the need to turn left across oncoming traffic to reach a ramp. It can feel strange the first time, so follow the lane lines and signals closely, keep your speed down, and do not try to change lanes while crossing over. The markings will guide you back to the right side.

lines.text: May you use it to pass?

narration.text: Here is a quick check: traffic in your lane is crawling, and the center turn lane is completely empty for the next two blocks. You want to drive along it until your turn. May you? Decide before reading on. No. A two-way left-turn lane is only for drivers turning left; you may wait in it until the turn is safe, but you may not use it to pass or to travel. Enter it just before your turn. And if the lane is marked with double broken yellow lines and overhead lights, it may be a reversible lane instead, so read the signals.

lines.text: Center turn lane: wait to turn left.

narration.text: Let us review. A two-way left-turn lane is only for drivers turning left from either direction; you may wait in it, but not pass or travel in it. If a street has a shared center turn lane, every left turn must be made from it. Reversible lanes carry traffic in different directions at different times and are set apart by a barrier or double broken yellow lines, sometimes with signs or lights, so check before entering. A diverging diamond interchange shifts traffic to the opposite side across the interchange so vehicles can reach ramps without interruption. Next, roundabouts.

why_how.text: Roundabouts keep traffic moving in one direction, so most conflicts are simple merges rather than crossings.
Large vehicles need extra room to turn, which is why the law gives them priority in roundabouts.

scenario.text: Lia approaches a roundabout as a delivery truck is entering from the next entry to her left, and a pedestrian waits at the crosswalk.

reasoning.text: Yield to large vehicles first, give way to the pedestrian in the crosswalk, and yield to circulating traffic from the left.

result.text: Lia lets the pedestrian cross, waits for the truck, then merges into a gap and signals before exiting.

claim.text: Common mistake: thinking drivers entering a roundabout have the right of way over circulating traffic.

correction.text: Drivers entering yield to traffic already circulating, which comes from the left.

memory_support.text: Big first, circling next, walkers always.

prompt.text: You are entering a roundabout and a bus is already driving in it. Who yields?

rationale.text: Large vehicles come first, then circulating traffic on the left, and crosswalk users whenever you enter or leave.

narration.text: Roundabouts are becoming common across Colorado, and they work well when every driver follows the same rules. This lesson covers which way traffic moves, who yields to whom when you enter, why large vehicles get special priority, how to treat pedestrians and bicyclists in crosswalks, and when to use your turn signal. The yielding rules come in layers, so we will build them step by step and then put them in order. By the end, you should be able to approach any roundabout calmly and know exactly whom to watch for and when you may merge.

In a roundabout, traffic circles to the right around a center island. Drivers entering yield to traffic already circulating. So the vehicles already in the circle have the right of way, and you look for a safe gap before merging in. Because everyone travels in the same direction, there are no left turns across oncoming traffic, which is why roundabouts usually have fewer serious crashes than regular intersections. Approach at a slow speed, look to your left for circulating traffic, and merge smoothly into a gap. Once you are in, keep moving with the flow until your exit.

lines.text: Yield to trucks, buses, emergency vehicles, RVs.
Entering, leaving or driving in it.
Two large vehicles: right yields to left.

narration.text: Colorado law requires you to yield to a truck, bus, emergency vehicle or recreational vehicle that is entering, leaving or driving in a roundabout. Large vehicles need extra room and may use more than one lane, or drive over the raised apron around the center island, to make the turn. Do not drive beside a large vehicle in a roundabout. When two such large vehicles meet there, the one on the right yields to the one on the left. For most drivers, the practical rule is simple: if a large vehicle is in or near the roundabout, give it the space it needs and wait.

lines.text: Yield to traffic from the left.
Do not stop fully unless needed.

narration.text: When you approach a roundabout with no large trucks present, yield to traffic coming from the left, which is the circulating traffic. Do not stop fully unless traffic keeps you from merging. Stopping at an empty roundabout entrance confuses the drivers behind you and can cause rear-end crashes. Instead, slow down, look left, and if there is a gap, merge into it without stopping. If traffic is heavy, stop at the yield line and wait for a gap. Smooth, predictable entry is what makes roundabouts work, so keep your speed low and your eyes on the traffic to your left.

lines.text: Give way to people in crosswalks.
Signal to change lanes and exit.

narration.text: Each time you enter or exit a roundabout, give way to anyone walking or riding in a crosswalk and to vehicles already circling. Crosswalks are usually set back from the circle at each entry and exit, so watch for pedestrians both as you approach and as you leave. Use your turn signals to change lanes and to exit. Signaling your exit tells waiting drivers and pedestrians that you are leaving the circle, so they can plan their own moves. Leaving a roundabout without signaling forces others to guess, which slows everyone down and invites conflicts.

lines.text: Then circulating traffic on the left.
Crosswalk users at every entry and exit.

narration.text: Here is the trap. Roundabout yielding has layers, and questions test them by mixing them up. Large vehicles come first: yield to trucks, buses, emergency vehicles and recreational vehicles. Next, yield to circulating traffic on the left. And give way to crosswalk users whenever you enter or leave, not just when entering. A tempting wrong answer says entering traffic has priority, or that pedestrians only matter at the exit. Hold the order in your head as big, circling, then walkers, and remember the walkers rule applies at both ends of your trip through the circle.

Here is a quick check: you are about to enter a roundabout, and a city bus is already driving around the circle toward your entry. A pedestrian is also waiting at the crosswalk where you will exit. Who yields, and to whom? Decide before reading on. You yield to the bus, because Colorado law requires you to yield to a bus, truck, emergency vehicle or recreational vehicle in a roundabout. Then merge into a gap in traffic from the left. When you reach your exit, give way to the pedestrian in the crosswalk, and signal as you leave.

lines.text: Walkers at every entry and exit.

narration.text: Let us close the chapter. In a roundabout, traffic circles to the right around a center island, and entering drivers yield to circulating traffic. Yield to trucks, buses, emergency vehicles and recreational vehicles entering, leaving or driving in it, and when two large vehicles meet, the one on the right yields to the one on the left. With no large trucks present, yield to traffic from the left and do not stop fully unless needed. Each time you enter or exit, give way to crosswalk users and circling vehicles, and signal to change lanes and exit. Next chapter: right of way.
